stops.name: Córdoba, birth on the eve of Passover
stops.campa: Moses ben Maimon is born in Córdoba, capital of al-Andalus, on the eve of Passover, a Sabbath, an hour and a third past noon, so the chronicles of his house will reckon it for centuries after. His father Maimon ben Joseph, dayyan of the city and pupil of Joseph ibn Migash, receives him into a lineage of judges reaching back, tradition says, to the House of David. Córdoba still wears the splendor of the Caliphate: horseshoe arches, a library of hundreds of thousands of volumes, three faiths reading the same Aristotle in different tongues.

stops.name: Córdoba, the dayyan's house and the double curriculum
stops.campa: In his father's house in the Jewish quarter, hard by the Great Mosque, the boy is set to two curricula at once: Mishnah and Talmud at Maimon's knee, and, through the window the Caliphate has left ajar, the sciences of the Arabs, mathematics, astronomy, logic, the medicine of Galen filtered through Baghdad and Córdoba's own physicians. He reads Aristotle already in Arabic translation before he has left off reciting the Shema as a child. The convivencia that will make him legend is, for now, simply his schooling.

stops.name: Córdoba, the Almohads take the city
stops.campa: In the spring the armies of the Almohads, the Berber reformers who preach the absolute oneness of God under Ibn Tumart's doctrine, take Córdoba from the fractured taifas. Where the Almoravids tolerated the protected communities, the new masters offer one law only: recite the shahada, or die, or go. Maimon's family will not apostatize and will not stay to be martyred; they choose the road. Moses is not yet eleven by some reckonings, thirteen by others, when the house of the dayyan closes its door on the city of his birth for the last time.

stops.name: The wandering, hidden years in Iberia
stops.campa: For a decade the family's road is hard to trace: the sources give hints of Almería, then still held by the Christian king Alfonso VII and so, for a family fleeing the Almohads, an island of relative safety on the Andalusian coast. Here, tradition holds, Moses continues his study of medicine and the philosophers, perhaps under teachers formed in the same school that produced Ibn Rushd, his own townsman and near-contemporary, though the two are never recorded meeting. No responsum, no signed page survives from these years: only the silence of a family in hiding, waiting out a storm that does not pass.

stops.name: Almería, the embarkation for the Maghreb
stops.campa: In 1157 Almería itself falls back under Almohad power, and the family's refuge closes. Within a year or two Maimon takes his sons aboard a ship out of the port, crossing the strait not toward safety in Christian Castile but, strangely, toward the very heart of Almohad territory: Fez, where a Jewish community still lives, camouflaged, under the eye of the caliph himself. It is a choice later ages find hard to credit, but the logic of hidden coexistence, professing what one does not believe in order to buy time to think and write, will define the coming years of Moses's life.

stops.name: Fez, arrival among the Almohads
stops.campa: The family settles at Fez, capital of the Almohad Maghreb and mother-city of the very doctrine that drove them from Spain, reasoning that a family unknown in a great capital draws less notice than one conspicuous in a small Andalusian town. They live, most historians judge, as outward Muslims, reciting in public what they do not believe, keeping the Sabbath and the dietary law behind closed doors. It is a role that will haunt Moses's later legal writing, for he alone among the great rabbinic authorities will have first-hand knowledge of what dissimulation under the sword actually costs a soul.

stops.name: Fez, the Epistle on Sanctification of the Name
stops.campa: A rabbi elsewhere in the Almohad lands has ruled that any Jew who merely recites the Muslim confession of faith under threat of death, without believing it, is already an apostate, lost even if he dies rather than repeat it twice. Moses, watching his own community strain under exactly this pressure, writes the Iggeret HaShmad, arguing the opposite: better to save one's life by outward conformity and flee at the first chance than to court a martyrdom the law does not in fact demand. It is his first great public act, and the most personal.

stops.name: Fez, the martyrdom of the teacher ibn Susan
stops.campa: Yehuda ha-Kohen ibn Susan, a scholar under whom Moses has studied and a leader of the hidden community, is denounced, hauled before the Almohad authorities, and put to death for refusing, openly this time, to affirm Islam. The killing tears away the last illusion of safety: if a man of ibn Susan's learning and discretion can be caught out and executed, no one in Fez is beyond reach. Within months the family determines what it has perhaps long known it must do: leave the Maghreb entirely, sailing east toward Palestine, where the Crusader kingdom at least does not ask a Jew to unsay his faith.

stops.name: Fez, the flight by night
stops.campa: On the night following the Sabbath, the fourth of Iyar, the family slips out of Fez toward the coast, leaving behind whatever cannot be carried and a decade of learned disguise. Moses will note the date precisely years later, as he notes every date of this journey, for a man who has just escaped a capital sentence for his faith does not forget the day of his deliverance. Ahead lies a crossing of the western Mediterranean in ships that do not always arrive, toward a Holy Land only lately stable enough under its Crusader kings to receive Jewish pilgrims at all.

stops.name: At sea, the storm and the vow
stops.campa: Between the Maghreb and Palestine the ship runs into a storm violent enough that everyone aboard believes death at hand: great waves rise over the deck and very nearly drown them all. It is the Sabbath, the tenth of Iyar, and Moses will set the date down afterward as exactly as a judge records a verdict. He vows to keep that day forever as a fast, for himself and his household and their descendants after them, a private day of dread against the sea. The feasting he reserves for whatever day the ship finally makes harbor.
stops.quote: On Shabbat, on the 10th of the month of Iyar, in the year 4925 since the time of creation, we were confronted with great waves which nearly drowned us all, as a violent storm arose at sea.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' own colophon note on the sea voyage, 1165

stops.name: Acre, the deliverance
stops.campa: On Sunday, the third of Sivan, the ship makes the port of Akko in peace, and Moses, his father, and his brother David step onto the soil of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, out of both the Almohad sword and the sea's hazard in a single crossing. He sets this date apart forever: a day of joy and feasting for himself and his household, marked with charity to the poor, kept, he charges his descendants, until the end of time. Acre's small Jewish community, established under the Franks, receives the refugees of Fez as men returned from the dead.
stops.quote: On Sunday, the 3rd of the month of Sivan, I left the ship in peace at the port of Akko, having been delivered from destruction and arrived in the land of Israel.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' own colophon note on his arrival at Acre, 1165

stops.name: Jerusalem, prayer on the Temple Mount
stops.campa: Five months after landing, Moses goes up to Jerusalem, held now by the Latin kings, and ascends the Haram, the platform of the ruined Temple, where a mosque and a shrine stand over the site of the Holy of Holies. He enters what he calls the Great and Holy House and prays there, fulfilling in his own body the psalmist's wish to behold the pleasantness of the Lord and visit in His sanctuary. It is Thursday, the sixth of Marcheshvan; he will keep this day too as a private festival, twinned three days later with an even holier ground.
stops.quote: I entered the Great and Holy House and prayed there, on Thursday, the 6th of the month of Marcheshvan.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' colophon note on his visit to Jerusalem, 1165
